e.head: сказа́ть
e.ety: Perfective form of archaic Russian каза́ть (kazátʹ), from Proto-Slavic *kazati.
phrases: so to speak (in a manner of speaking)

e.head: говори́ть
e.ety: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *govoriti, from Proto-Indo-European *gewH- (“to call, cry”) with a *-b⁽ʰ⁾- enlargement, perhaps connected to the synonymous *ǵʰewH-. Cognate to Polish gaworzyć, Czech hovořit, Ukrainian говорити (hovoryty), Serbo-Croatian гово̀рити, Persian گفتن (goftan, “to say, to speak”).

g: to say (repeatedly or frequently); iterative of говори́ть (govorítʹ)
to articulate, to pronounce, to utter
to reserve for oneself, to stipulate, to set as a condition (in a contract, transaction, etc.)
to censure, to reprimand, to rebuke
to articulate, to pronounce, to utter
to tell off, to reprimand, to lecture
reproof; reprimand; rebuke, scolding; dressing down, admonition
the sound of talking, the sound of voices, the sound of speech

e.head: говору́н
e.ety: By surface analysis, говори́ть (govorítʹ, “to speak, to talk”) + -ун (-un, frequentive-agentive suffix).

phrases: pretend, affect (to make a false display of)

e.ety: Inherited from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n)-, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱom. See Proto-Slavic *sъ(n) for more information. The /n/ persists in снять (snjatʹ) (originally a prefixed derivative of ять (jatʹ, “to take”)), from which other words in -нять (-njatʹ) were produced by rebracketing. See also с (s), Old East Slavic съ (sŭ), and compare the analogous loss of -n- in в- (v-).

e.ety: Inherited from Old East Slavic въ- (vŭ-), from Proto-Slavic *vъ(n)-, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁én. The /n/ persists in внять (vnjatʹ). See also в (v), Old East Slavic въ (vŭ), Proto-Slavic *vъ(n). Compare the similar development in с- (s-) from Proto-Slavic *sъ(n)-.

g: third-person masculine singular pronoun: he, it.

e.ety: Inherited from Old East Slavic онъ (onŭ), from Proto-Slavic *onъ, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *anas, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂énos (“that”). Inflected forms from Old East Slavic и (i), from Proto-Slavic *jь, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *is, from Proto-Indo-European *ís and Proto-Indo-European *Hyós. See о́ный (ónyj).
